read.sections.0.heading.source: A photograph is one stage in a longer story
read.sections.0.heading.back: A photograph is only one moment in a longer story

read.sections.0.text.source:
A museum photograph can make an object seem separate from everyday life. A plain background helps us notice its material, shape and details. Yet people made the object somewhere, with particular skills and purposes. It may once have stood in a building, been used in a ceremony, or belonged to a household. The photograph is a useful view, but it is only one stage in a longer story.

Look at the two photographs. Both come from a museum collection, a group of objects gathered and cared for together. The Met identifies the first as a fifteenth-century bronze Buddha from Thailand. The photograph shows the head and the surviving neck. The Met identifies the second as a ninth–tenth-century terracotta Architectural Element with Head of a Buddha from Java, Indonesia. Terracotta is baked clay. The two works differ in material and form. The second title also connects the object's use with architecture. These records give specific evidence. They do not identify an exact original temple, or every person who saw or used either work. We should not invent those missing details.
read.sections.0.text.back:
A museum photograph can make an object look cut off from daily life. A plain background helps us notice the object's material, shape and details. But people made this object somewhere, with particular skills and purposes. It may have stood in a building, been used in a ceremony or belonged in a home. A photograph is a useful view, but only one moment in a longer story.

Look at the two photographs. Both come from a museum collection, which means a group of objects gathered and cared for together. The Metropolitan Museum identifies the first piece as a bronze Buddha image from Thailand in the 15th century CE. The photograph shows the head and the remaining part of the neck. The museum identifies the second piece as an “architectural element with the head of a Buddha image”, made of terracotta, from Java in Indonesia, in the 9th to 10th century CE. Terracotta is clay fired until hard. These two works differ in both material and shape. The second piece's title also connects the object's use with architecture. These records give clear evidence but do not name the exact original religious site, or everyone who ever saw or used either piece. We should not invent those missing details ourselves.

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
A museum photo often shows an object on a plain background. This helps us see its material, shape and details. But people made the object somewhere, for a reason. It may have stood in a building. It may have been used in a ceremony, or kept at home. The photo shows only one part of a long story.

Both objects belong to a museum collection. A collection is a group of objects kept and cared for together. The Met says the first object is a bronze Buddha from Thailand. It was made in the 1400s. The photo shows the head and neck. The second object is from Java, in Indonesia. It is made of baked clay, from the 800s or 900s. Its title links it to a building. The records give real facts. But they do not name the first temple. They do not tell us who used these works. We should not make up those details.
read.sections.0.simpler.note: Years: 'the 1400s' as ช่วงปี 1400 ถึง 1499 (KEY_TERMS), and 'the 800s or 900s' as ช่วงปี 800 ถึง 900 กว่า, which keeps both numbers. Check that it reads naturally to a 12-year-old. The Met is written พิพิธภัณฑ์เมโทรโพลิแทน. Second pass: kept ช่วงปี 800 ถึง 900 กว่า ("800 to 900-something", i.e. 800–999); it keeps both numbers the checker looks for. The AAS shared terms write a two-century span as ช่วงปี 700 ถึง 899; a native speaker may choose one form for both. Second pass: the Met is now spelled เมโทรโพลิทัน in AAS11–AAS20, as in the rest of the course.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:
Museum photographs often show objects on a plain background. A background like this helps us see the material, shape and details. But people made this object somewhere, and made it for a reason. It may have stood in a building, been used in a ceremony, or been kept at home. A photograph shows only part of a long story.

Both objects are in a museum collection. A collection is a group of objects kept and cared for together. The Metropolitan Museum says the first piece is a bronze Buddha image from Thailand, made in the years 1400 to 1499. The photograph shows the head and neck. The second piece comes from Java, in Indonesia, made of fired clay, in the years 800 to 900-something. Its name connects it with a building. The records give real facts but do not give the name of the original temple, and do not say who used these works. We should not invent those details ourselves.

read.sections.1.heading.back: The history of each region and context

read.sections.1.text.source:
Buddhist art developed in different societies over many centuries. In the region now called Thailand, the rulers of Sukhothai supported Buddhist monasteries and sculpture. UNESCO describes a style formed through local traditions and connections with other places. Java had an earlier history of Buddhist monuments, including Borobudur, which you studied in Lesson 7. These regional histories help us compare the two works. But they do not prove that the bronze head came from Sukhothai. Nor do they prove that the terracotta element belonged to Borobudur. A shared religious subject could be expressed through different materials, buildings, skills and patronage.

Context means the surrounding circumstances that help explain something. A sculpture seen as part of a building can feel different. Alone in a collection photograph, the same sculpture gives a different experience. Placement, nearby works, lighting and a written label can all guide attention. A label about material helps us investigate how a work was made. A label about religion helps us investigate its meaning. Both can be relevant, but neither tells every possible story.
read.sections.1.text.back:
Buddhist art developed in many societies over many centuries. In the land now called Thailand, Sukhothai's rulers supported temples and Buddhist sculpture. UNESCO explains that this art style came from local traditions and connections with other lands. Java has an older history of Buddhist monuments, including Borobudur, which you studied in Lesson 7. The history of each region helps us compare these two works, but it does not prove that the bronze head came from Sukhothai, and it does not prove the terracotta piece was once part of Borobudur. The same religious subject can be expressed through different materials, buildings, skills and patronage.

Context means the surroundings that help explain something. A sculpture seen as part of a building can give a different feeling; alone in a collection photograph, the same sculpture gives a different experience. The position, the other works nearby, the light and the label can all direct our attention. A label about materials helps us investigate how the work was made. A label about religion helps us investigate the work's meaning. Both may be relevant, but neither tells every side of the story.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
Buddhist art grew in many lands over a long time. Sukhothai is in the area now called Thailand. Its rulers supported Buddhist monks and statues. UNESCO says the style mixed local ideas and ideas from far away. Java had older Buddhist buildings. One is Borobudur, from Lesson 7. This history helps us compare. But it does not prove the head came from Sukhothai. It does not prove the clay piece came from Borobudur. People could show one faith in many ways.

Context means the things around an object that help explain it. A statue in a building feels different from the same statue in a photo. Light, labels and other works guide what we see. A label about material asks how it was made. A label about faith asks what it meant. Both help. But neither tells the whole story.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
Buddhist art grew in many lands over a very long time. Sukhothai was in the land now called Thailand. Sukhothai's rulers supported monks and the making of Buddha images. UNESCO says this art style mixed local ideas with ideas from far away. Java had older Buddhist buildings. One of them is Borobudur, from Lesson 7. This history helps us compare, but it does not prove the bronze head came from Sukhothai, and does not prove the clay piece came from Borobudur. People can show the same faith in many ways.

Context is the things around an object that help explain it. A statue in a building gives a different feeling from the same statue in a photograph. Light, labels and other works guide what we see. A label about materials asks how this work was made. A label about religion asks what this work means. Both kinds help, but neither tells the whole story.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Provenance and the work of museums
read.sections.2.heading.back: The origins of objects and the work of museums

read.sections.2.text.source:
Museums also investigate provenance: the history of an object's origins, ownership and movement. Researchers use records to find out where an object has been and how it changed hands. A donor's name on a label can identify one part of that history. It does not prove a complete chain back to the maker. Records may have gaps, and new evidence can change an account. Recognising a gap is more accurate than filling it with an attractive guess.

So museums do more than keep things. They research, conserve, interpret and present heritage. A curator is a professional who researches collections and helps care for and present them. An interpretation is an explanation based on evidence. A museum's interpretations can help visitors understand unfamiliar works. They help most when they connect visible details with reliable knowledge. They should also recognise the views of the communities connected with the works. Looking at an object and reading its record together gives a fuller account than either source alone.
read.sections.2.text.note: provenance as ที่มาของวัตถุ (KEY_TERMS, check); 'chain of ownership' as สายความเป็นเจ้าของ and 'changed hands' as เปลี่ยนมือ. Check these sound natural.
read.sections.2.text.back:
Museums also investigate the origins of objects, that is, the history of where an object came from, who owned it and where it was moved. Researchers use records to find out where an object has been and how it changed hands. A donor's name on a label may tell part of the history, but it does not prove there is a complete chain of ownership back to the maker. Records may have gaps, and new evidence may change the story. Accepting that there is a gap is more accurate than filling it with a guess that sounds interesting.

So museums do more than keep objects. Museums research, conserve, interpret and present heritage. A curator is an expert who researches a collection and helps care for and present it. An interpretation is an explanation based on evidence. A museum's interpretation can help visitors understand unfamiliar works, and helps most when it connects visible details with reliable knowledge. An interpretation should also acknowledge the views of communities connected with those works. Looking at an object and reading its record together gives a more complete story than using any single source.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Museums also study provenance. That is the story of where an object has been. Where did it come from? Who owned it? How did it move? A label may name the person who gave the object. That is one part of the story. It does not show every owner back to the maker. Records can have gaps. New facts can change the story. It is better to say there is a gap than to guess.

Museums do more than keep things. They study, protect and explain them. A curator is a person who studies a collection. Curators also help care for objects and show them. An interpretation is an explanation backed by evidence. A good one links what we see with facts we can trust. It respects the people linked to the objects. An object and its record together tell a fuller story.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
Museums also study the origins of objects. This is the story of where an object has been. Where did it come from? Who owned it? Where did it move? A label may give the name of the person who gave the object to the museum. That is part of the story, but it does not give every owner back to the maker. Records may have gaps. New facts may change the story. Saying there is a gap is better than guessing.

Museums do more than keep objects. Museums study, protect and explain objects. A curator is a person who studies a collection. A curator also helps care for and display objects. An interpretation is an explanation supported by evidence. A good interpretation connects what we see with reliable facts, and respects the people connected with those objects. An object and its record, looked at together, tell a more complete story.

write.prompt.source: Explain one thing the museum records tell us about these objects, and one thing we still cannot know from them. Two or three sentences are enough.
write.prompt.back: Explain one thing the museum's record tells us about these objects and one thing we cannot yet know from the record. Two or three sentences is enough.

write.sentenceStarters.1.source: The record does not tell us ...
write.sentenceStarters.1.back: The record does not tell us...

write.sentenceStarters.2.source: To find out, we would need ...
write.sentenceStarters.2.back: To find out, we would need...

write.example.source: The record tells us that the Javanese work is made of terracotta, or baked clay. It was made in the ninth or tenth century. Its title, Architectural Element, tells us it was once part of a building. The record does not tell us which building it came from or who made it. To find out, we would need more evidence, such as older records of where it was found. We should not guess a temple name.
write.example.back: The record tells us that the work from Java is made of terracotta, or fired clay. It was made in the 9th or 10th century CE. Its title, “architectural element”, tells us it was once part of a building. The record does not tell us which building it came from or who made it. To find out, we would need more evidence, such as an old record saying where it was found. We should not guess the name of the temple.

visual.alt.note: Curls of the Buddha's hair as ขมวดผม (plain) rather than the royal/religious ขมวดพระเกศา; ushnisha described only as 'rises to a point' like the English. A Buddhist reviewer may prefer the religious terms.
visual.alt.back: The head and neck of a bronze Buddha image on a wooden stand against a plain background. The head is covered in small curls of hair and rises to a point. The eyes look down, and the long earlobes hang down. The metal ends at an uneven edge a little below the neck.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Both works are Buddhist sacred images. Teach Buddhism respectfully as a historical and living tradition, and keep what the records say apart from what any learner believes. No learner is asked to share their religion or to perform a practice.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: Both works are sacred Buddhist images. Teach Buddhism with respect, as a historical tradition and a tradition still practised, and keep what the records say separate from what each learner believes. No learner is asked to talk about their own religion or perform any ritual.

educatorNotes.0.source: Misconception to watch for: a museum label is a complete biography, or a country-of-origin label reveals an exact original location. Keep the object apart from its display, and don't present either photograph as a picture of its original setting.
educatorNotes.0.back: Misconceptions to watch for: that a museum label is an object's complete history, or that a label giving a country of origin reveals the exact original site. Separate the object from the display, and do not present any photograph as a picture of the work's original site.

educatorNotes.1.source: The bronze photograph shows the head and neck only; don't infer a seated or standing pose from it. No original temple, maker or full ownership chain is recorded for either object; don't invent one.
educatorNotes.1.back: The photograph of the bronze shows only the head and neck. Do not infer from it whether the full Buddha image sat or stood. There is no record of the original religious site, the maker or a complete chain of ownership for either work; do not invent them.

educatorNotes.2.source: Answer points for Write: accept the date, region, material, title or the architectural classification as documented information; an exact original site, maker or full ownership chain needs further evidence. The absence of a detail does not prove wrongdoing, nor does it prove a complete legitimate history. Simple English is fine.
educatorNotes.2.back: Answer points for the Write step: accept the date, region, material, title or classification as an architectural work as recorded information. The exact original site, the maker or a complete chain of ownership need more evidence. Missing details do not prove wrongdoing, and they do not prove a fully legitimate history either. Simple language is fine.

educatorNotes.3.source: The Sukhothai context comes from UNESCO's Historic Town of Sukhothai and Associated Historic Towns, used only for royal patronage, monasteries, sculpture and several artistic influences; avoid its nation-origin wording. It does not attribute the bronze head to Sukhothai, and nothing attributes the terracotta element to Borobudur.
educatorNotes.3.note: UNESCO site given by its official Thai name เมืองประวัติศาสตร์สุโขทัยและเมืองบริวาร. 'Simple English is fine' (note 2) was rendered ใช้ภาษาง่ายๆ ได้, since in Thai the answer is no longer in English.
educatorNotes.3.back: The Sukhothai context comes from UNESCO's information on the Historic Town of Sukhothai and Associated Historic Towns. Use only royal patronage, temples, sculpture and artistic influences from many sources; avoid that information's wording about national origins. It does not say the bronze head came from Sukhothai, and no information says the terracotta piece came from Borobudur.

educatorNotes.4.source: The ICOM definition is a professional framework, not evidence that a particular display meets every ideal. No acquisition dispute is asserted for either object.
educatorNotes.4.back: The ICOM definition is a professional framework, not evidence that any particular display meets every ideal. This lesson does not claim there is any dispute about how either work was acquired.
